findings: 6100 Fleet fuel: S4 says fuel 'declined $17,500'. It rose. 91,200 to 108,700 is a $17,500 increase, +19.2%. The direction is backwards and the sentence as written would have a reader believe cost came out of the month.

6100 Fleet fuel: S5 concedes roughly $9,800 of July fuel will be invoiced in August. That expense is incurred in July and belongs in July. Add it back and fuel is 118,500, a variance of $27,300 on 91,200 or 29.9%, which clears both the $25,000 and the 10 percent gate. Correctly accrued, this line requires commentary and does not have any that survives.

6000 Warehouse wages: S6 says wages rose $74,900. The table variance is $79,400 (702,500 to 781,900). The memo is $4,500 light, and $74,900 is June interest expense on line 7100, which is where I suspect the figure was picked up from.

6200 Repairs and maintenance, depots: S7 and S8 cannot both be true. S7 says the depot repair program closed in June with no further repair spend expected this year. S8 books $36,400 of July repairs as phase two of the Southline dock program. One of these sentences is wrong and either way the $36,400 is unexplained.

5000 Cost of product sold: S3 blames the $147,000 decline on renegotiated inbound freight rates. Inbound freight is its own account, 5100, and the memo's own definition excludes inbound freight from cost of product sold. The driver is attached to the wrong account.

5000 Cost of product sold: the freight story also fails on margin. June margin is (5,612,000 - 4,278,000) / 5,612,000 = 23.8%. July is (5,398,000 - 4,131,000) / 5,398,000 = 23.5%. An input cost win lifts margin. Cost fell 3.4% while revenue fell 3.8%, so cost came down slower than volume and margin lost about 30 basis points. No one mentions margin at all.

5100 Inbound freight: down $43,500, -15.1%, marked over threshold, and never explained on its own line. A 15.1% drop against a 3.4% decline in product cost is out of proportion to volume, and given the cutoff habit admitted in S5 I want to know whether a July freight invoice is sitting unbooked the same way the fuel invoice is.

6400 Bad debt expense: down $52,500 to $9,500, -84.7%, over the threshold, and there is not one sentence about it. Bad debt falling 85% while revenue is declining is a reserve question, and an unexplained reserve release straight into earnings is exactly the item a reader needs named.

7200 Inventory shrink adjustment: up $62,300 to $71,200, +700%, over the threshold, and silent. This is the largest percentage move on the page and it goes unaddressed while fleet fuel, which is under the threshold, gets two sentences.

6600 Marketing and trade shows: S9 books $96,400 in July for a trade show held in September and offers that as the explanation. That is a statement that the cost sits in the wrong period. Either it should be in prepaid until September or the sentence needs to say why a September event is a July expense.

6600 Marketing against 6100 Fleet fuel: the memo runs two opposite cutoff policies in the same page. S5 defends leaving a July fuel cost out of July. S9 defends putting a September show cost into July. Both cannot be the company's practice.

7100 Interest expense: S10 says interest rose 1.9 percent 'or $1,900'. The table variance is $1,400 (74,900 to 76,300), and 1.9% of 74,900 is $1,423. The $1,900 appears nowhere in the table and does not reconcile to the percentage the same sentence quotes.

S11 operating expense ratio: recomputed, it did not hold. June opex (6000 through 7200) is 702,500 + 91,200 + 118,600 + 62,000 + 22,000 + 74,900 + 8,900 = $1,080,100 on total revenue of $6,774,000, or 15.9%. July is 781,900 + 108,700 + 36,400 + 9,500 + 96,400 + 76,300 + 71,200 = $1,180,400 on $6,622,500, or 17.8%. That is a 190 basis point deterioration, and rounding does not rescue it because the rounded figures are 16% and 18%.

S11 'the cost base moved with volume': operating expense rose $100,300 while total revenue fell $151,500 (6,774,000 to 6,622,500). Cost moved opposite to volume. The conclusion is the reverse of what the numbers show, and it is the one sentence a reader would take away.

4000 Product revenue: S1 asserts the decline is 'consistent with the same month last year'. There is no prior year column anywhere in the table, so the reader cannot test the claim. A comparison that carries the whole seasonality argument has to show its figure.

4100 Service revenue: at $55,000 and 5.3% this line fails the stated test, which requires both $25,000 and 10 percent, yet it gets a full sentence in S2 while 6400 bad debt and 7200 shrink, which both clear the test, get nothing. The memo is spending its space on the wrong lines.

4200 Freight billed to customers: up $7,500, +6.2%, while inbound freight cost on 5100 fell $43,500, -15.1%, and product revenue fell 3.8%. Billing customers more for freight while freight cost drops sharply and volume declines is not explained anywhere, and it points back at whether 5100 is complete.
